full_judgment:
This Rule is directed against the judgment and order dated 20-7-88 passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 53 of 1985 by the Subordinate Judge, Kurigram reversing those dated 28-12-83 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 46 of 1983 by the Upazila Munsif, Nageswari and sending the case back on remand. 

 2. The pre-emptor-petitioner instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 43 of 1979 (re-numbered as Miscellaneous case No.46 of 1983) in the Court of the Munsif, Kurigram for pre-emption of the case land against the opposite parties contending, inter alia, that he is a co-sharer by purchase of the disputed holding as well as contiguous land holder, that the opposite parties are strangers and they purchased the case land from Abbas Ali on 25-9-78 without notice to him under section 89 of the EBSA & T Act. 

 3. The opposite parties contested the case by filing written objection contending, inter alia, that the petitioner became co-sharer by kabala purchase, as such, the application for pre-emption is competent. 

 4. The Upazila Munsif heard Miscellaneous Case No. 47 of 1983 brought by the same petitioner analogously with two other Miscellaneous Cases i.e. 62 and 63 of 1983 brought by the opposite parties as pre-emptor by judgment and order dated 28-12-83 allowing Miscellaneous Case Nos. 46 and 47 of 1983 while rejecting the Miscellaneous Case Nos. 62 and 63 of 1983 on proper consideration of the facts, circumstances and the evidence on record. 

 5. On appeal being Miscellaneous Appeal No.53 of 1985 by the pre-emptees, the Subordinate Judge, Kurigram allowed the appeal by order dated 20-7-88 and sent the case back on remand for fresh trial on the ground that the deposition sheets were not signed by the presiding Judge and, as such, the same has no legal effect. 

 6. Mr. Bikash Paul, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the mere fact that the witnesses depositions were not signed by the Judge will not vitiate the trial. It was at best an irregularity under section 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in respect of this contention he has cited the case of Delhi Development Authority vs. Shiv Charan reported in AIR 1979 (Delhi) 22. In the cited case it was held that the omission to sign the depositions is a defect or irregularity in the proceedings. But the merits of the case or the jurisdiction of the Court are not affected by the omission. A decision of a Court cannot be upset merely for technical and immaterial defects. Noncompliance of rule 5 of Order 18 does not destroy the validity of the whole proceeding. Rule 5 is a rule of procedure. Rules of procedure are made to sub-serve the ends of justice and not to defeat them. Section 99 aims to prevent technicalities from over-coming the ends of justice. In that case reference was made to AIR 1957 (Patna) 293 and AIR 1954 (SC) 340. 

 7. In the facts and circumstances of the present case, I am of the opinion that the Subordinate Judge. Kurigram was not right in setting aside the decree on this technical ground as it did not afford any ground for re-trial since there is no doubt whatsoever that the depositions were recorded in presence of the parties by the presiding Judge himself. No one alleged that the depositions were wrongly recorded or that the witnesses did not appear in the court below. 

 9. In view of the above discussions. I hold that the Subordinate Judge by sending the case back on remand for fresh trial committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 In the result, the Rule is made absolute. There will be no order as to costs. The impugned order dated 20-7-88 passed in Misc. Appeal No. 53 of 1985 by the Subordinate Judge, Kurigram is set aside. The case is sent back on remand to the learned Subordinate Judge to hear the appeal and decide the same on merit. The order of stay passed earlier is hereby vacated.
